title: Top 10 Essential English Verbs for Absolute Beginners (A0–A1 / A2 Master Guide)
dek: A complete magazine spread for absolute beginners discovering English. Master the top 10 core verbs step-by-step (be, have, think, know, like, want/would like, work/study/learn, go/be going to, can, eat/drink) with full conjugations, usage patterns, and real-world sentence frames.

blocks.text: Introduction to the Top 10 Core Verbs

Welcome to Part 1 of our 2-part master verb guide for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! When you start learning English, you don't need thousands of words to start speaking. Frequency research demonstrates that just 10 core verbs carry up to 80% of daily spoken output. This 12-page issue gives every core verb its own dedicated page with clear grammar rules, practical sentence frames, real-world examples, and common traps to avoid.

🗺️ Interactive Verb Map: Part 1 Core Verbs

Flip through this issue page by page or jump directly to any verb spread:

1. To Be — Existence, identity, age, states, location.2. To Have — Possession, bodily states, routines.3. To Think — Opinions, thoughts, beliefs.4. To Know — Facts, familiarity, skills.5. To Like — Preferences, tastes, polite requests.6. To Want / Would Like — Desires, ordering, plans.7. To Work / Study / Learn — Occupation, studies, acquiring skills.8. To Go / Be Going To — Movement, travel, future.9. To Can (Modal) — Ability, requests, permission.10. To Eat / Drink — Food, beverages, dining, hydration.Outro & Practice — Language matrix & test tools.

COSYMAGAZINE • Vol. 2026.08 — Special Edition

BE — The little verb that does almost everything ✨

🗺️ Your learning route   🟢 A0–A1 · Start here: identity, age, feelings, descriptions, place, time.   🔵 A1–A2 · Build confidence: negatives, questions, possession, there is/are, everyday expressions.   🟣 A2+ · One step further: be as a helping verb. Keep this page as a reference—you do not need to memorise everything at once.

Meet be: am, is, are. It helps you say who someone is, how someone feels, where something is, what something is like, and what time or weather it is. English often needs be where another language may use a different structure. 💡 The trick is to learn the pattern with the meaning, not just the words.

rows: To be (am / is / are)
Identity, age, feelings, place
I am a student. / He is at home.
be on time, be quiet, be right
To have (have / has)
Possession, family, states
I have a car. / She has a sister.
have breakfast, have a shower, have a good day
To think
Opinions and thoughts
I think so. / What do you think?
think twice, think about, think of
To know
Facts, people, skills
I know the answer. / I know how to drive.
let me know, as far as I know, you know
To like
Preferences and taste
I like coffee. / Do you like sports?
like very much, would like, look like
To want / would like
Wishes and polite requests
I want water. / I would like tea, please.
want to learn, would like to order, if you want
To go / be going to
Movement and plans
I go to work. / We are going to eat.
go home, go shopping, go on foot
Can (modal)
Ability and permission
I can speak English. / Can you help me?
can I have…, as fast as I can, can do
To eat
Food and meals
I eat fruit. / Let’s eat out.
eat healthy, eat out, something to eat
To drink
Drinks and hydration
I drink water. / He drinks coffee.
drink water, a hot drink, something to drink

blocks.text: 01 · The three shapes of BE 🧩

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb BE
SubjectFull formShort formExample
II amI’mI’m ready.
YouYou areYou’reYou’re early.
HeHe isHe’sHe’s my brother.
SheShe isShe’sShe’s at home.
ItIt isIt’sIt’s cold.
WeWe areWe’reWe’re busy.
TheyThey areThey’reThey’re students.
💡 Pattern to remember: the subject chooses the form: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are. Short forms are very common in conversation. Use full forms when you want emphasis or a more formal tone.
02 · Ten everyday jobs for BE 🌟

🟢 A · Identity and names — say who someone is or identify a thing.
Pattern: subject + be + noun/name.
I’m Maya. He’s my brother, Leo. This is my new book.

🟢 B · Jobs and roles — use a/an with a singular countable job.
I’m an English teacher. She’s a doctor. He’s an IT specialist.
⚠️ Say a doctor / an actor, not she is doctor.

🟢 C · Age — English uses be, not have.
I’m 20 (years old). My parents are 55. How old are you?

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
I have 20 years.
I’m 20. (or I am 20 years old.)

🟢 D · Nationality and origin — use a nationality adjective or be from + place.
I’m French. He’s Spanish. We’re from Paris.
🔎 Nationality describes a person; from tells you their origin.

🟢 E · Descriptions and characteristics — be + adjective.
My friend is tall and funny. The cake is delicious. My room is clean today.
💡 Adjectives do not take a plural -s: They are happy, not they are happies.

🟢 F · Feelings and physical states — say how someone feels or what state they are in.
I’m happy to meet you. We’re hungry and thirsty. He’s tired today.
🗣️ Mini-dialogue: “Are you okay?” “Yes, I’m fine, thanks.”

🟢 G · Location and position — be + place/preposition.
I’m at home. She’s in the kitchen. The keys are on the table.
📍 Useful place words: in the room · on the table · under the bed · next to the café · behind the house · in front of the school · between two shops · near the station · at work/school.

🟢 H · Time, weather and dates — English commonly uses it is for time and weather.
It’s 11 o’clock. It’s cold and sunny. It’s Friday. Today is October 23.
💡 For dates, you can also say It’s October 23rd (especially in American English) or It’s the 23rd of October (common in British English).

🔵 I · Demonstratives and possession — this/that is for one thing; these/those are for more than one.
This is my bag. That is her sister. These are our books. Those are my parents.
⚖️ Be vs have: This bag is mine identifies the owner; I have a car says what I own.

🔵 J · Material, measurements and numbers — be can describe what something is made of, its price, size or distance.
The table is made of wood. The ticket is €10. The station is two kilometres away. My room is four metres wide.
🔎 In is made of, be is part of a passive structure—see “One step further” below.
03 · Make it negative 🚦
To make a negative, put not after am/is/are. You do not need do or does.

Negative conjugation forms table for verb BE
Full formShort formExample
am not’m notI’m not tired today.
is notisn’t / ’s notShe isn’t at school.
are notaren’t / ’re notThey aren’t hungry.

⚠️ Common Traps

• Say I’m not or I am not—standard English does not use I amn’t.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
She doesn’t be happy.
She isn’t happy.
04 · Ask yes/no questions ❓
Move am/is/are before the subject: You are ready. → Are you ready?

Yes and No questions and short answers table for verb BE
StatementQuestionYes, …No, …
You are ready.Are you happy?Yes, I am.No, I’m not.
He is a doctor.Is he a doctor?Yes, he is.No, he isn’t.
She is here.Is she here?Yes, she is.No, she isn’t.
It is cold.Is it cold?Yes, it is.No, it isn’t.
They are ready.Are they ready?Yes, they are.No, they aren’t.
💡 Short-answer rule: in positive short answers, use the full form: ✅ Yes, she is.   ❌ Yes, she’s. Negative short answers can use contractions: No, she isn’t.
05 · Ask for the detail: WH- questions 🔎

WH- question words and usage table for verb BE
Question wordWhat it asksExample
Whatthing / informationWhat is your name?
Whoperson / identityWho is she?
WhereplaceWhere are your keys?
Whentime / dateWhen is your birthday?
WhyreasonWhy are you sad?
Howstate / conditionHow are you today?
How oldageHow old is your brother?
How muchprice / amountHow much is this bag?

✨ Two questions that look similar—but do different jobs:
• What is your teacher like? → asks about personality or characteristics: She’s kind and funny.
• How is your grandfather? → asks about health or well-being: He’s fine, thanks.
06 · Say that something exists: THERE IS / THERE ARE 🏡
Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one. It is a useful way to talk about what you can see or what is available.

There is and there are sentence patterns table
MeaningPositiveNegativeQuestion
One thingThere is a chair.There isn’t a chair.Is there a chair?
More than oneThere are two chairs.There aren’t any chairs.Are there any chairs?
🗣️ In real life: Is there a bank near here? · There’s a café next to the station. · There are two free seats.
07 · Small words, big meaning: fixed expressions 💬

items: **be right / be wrong** — <mark class="example-chip">You’re right.</mark> <mark class="example-chip">I’m wrong.</mark>
**be afraid of / be sure** — <mark class="example-chip">She’s afraid of dogs.</mark> <mark class="example-chip">I’m sure it’s okay.</mark>
**be interested in / be good at** — <mark class="example-chip">He’s interested in music.</mark> <mark class="example-chip">She’s good at English.</mark>
**be late / early / ready / busy / free** — <mark class="example-chip">We’re late.</mark> <mark class="example-chip">Dinner is ready.</mark> <mark class="example-chip">I’m free tomorrow.</mark>

blocks.text: 🔎 Notice the prepositions that belong with some expressions: interested in, good at, afraid of. Learn them as little word groups.
08 · One step further: BE can be a helping verb 🟣 A2+
So far, be has carried the main meaning: She is happy. Sometimes, be helps another part of the sentence instead. You can recognise these patterns now and learn them gradually.

Helping verb patterns table for verb BE
PatternExampleWhat BE is doing
be + -ingShe is working.Helps form the present continuous: an action happening around now.
be + past participleThe table is made of wood.Helps form the passive: the sentence focuses on the thing or action, not the doer.
⚖️ Compare: She is happy = be describes her state. · She is working = is helps form the action verb working.
09 · Quick check 🎯

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence about age and a job.
options: She has 25 years and is doctor.
She is 25 and she is a doctor.
She is 25 and she has doctor.
blocks.explanation: Use **be** for age and put **a/an** before a singular countable job: *She is 25. She is a doctor.*

blocks.question: Choose the correct positive short answer: “Is she at home?”
blocks.explanation: Positive short answers use the full form: *Yes, she is.*

blocks.question: Complete the sentence: “___ there any cafés near here?”
blocks.explanation: Use **are** with the plural noun *cafés*: *Are there any cafés near here?*

blocks.question: Which sentence describes an action happening around now?
blocks.explanation: In *He is working*, **is + working** forms the present continuous. In the other sentences, *is* describes a state or identity.

blocks.text: 🌱 You do not have to master every pattern today. Start by noticing am / is / are, then practise one use at a time. The more examples you meet, the more natural BE will feel.

💌 Your COSY journey

You can now say who you are. Next, discover how to talk about the people and things that are part of your life.

Verb 2 — "To Have" (have / has)

The verb to have is one of the most essential verbs in English. At A0–A1 level, you use it to talk about possessions, family, physical characteristics, food and drink, daily activities, and health conditions.
There are two essential present simple forms to learn first: • have — I, you, we, they • has — he, she, it
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb HAVE
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI have a phone. / You have a nice house. / We have two children. / They have a new car.I don't have a car. / You don't have a pen. / We don't have time. / They don't have any pets.Do I have time? / Do you have a question? / Do we have class today? / Do they have tickets?
He / She / ItHe has a sister. / She has blue eyes. / It has four legs.He doesn't have a job. / She doesn't have a brother. / It doesn't have a name.Does he have a pet? / Does she have a car? / Does it have a camera?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third Person Conjugation

Use has only with he, she, and it in positive present simple sentences.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
She have a cat.
She has a cat.
2. Main Usages & Sentence Frames

items: **A. Possessions:** <mark class="example-chip">I have a new laptop.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has a red bicycle.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have a big house in Paris.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They have a friendly dog.</mark>

**B. Family & Relationships:** <mark class="example-chip">I have two brothers.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has a young daughter.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He has a big family.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have many good friends.</mark>

**C. Physical Characteristics:** <mark class="example-chip">I have brown eyes.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has long blonde hair.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He has a dark beard.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">The cat has a long tail.</mark>

**D. Things & Features:** <mark class="example-chip">The apartment has three bedrooms.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">The car has four doors.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">My phone has a great camera.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">The school has a large library.</mark>

**E. Problems & Needs:** <mark class="example-chip">I have a problem with my laptop.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has a bad headache.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have an urgent question.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He has a lot of work today.</mark>

**F. Time & Availability:** <mark class="example-chip">I have free time this afternoon.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have an important meeting today.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has an English lesson at 10 AM.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They have no money.</mark>

**G. Food & Drink (Action Meaning):** <mark class="example-chip">I have a delicious sandwich for lunch.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She has a cup of tea every morning.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have breakfast at 8 o'clock.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They have dinner together at home.</mark> (Here *have* means *eat* or *drink*).

blocks.text: 3. Negative Sentences (-) & The Base Verb Rule
To make negative sentences with have, use don't have or doesn't have.

Negative structure table for verb HAVE
SubjectNegative StructureExample Sentence
I / You / We / Theydon't haveI don't have any money. / We don't have class today.
He / She / Itdoesn't haveShe doesn't have a brother. / My phone doesn't have a good camera.

⚠️ Common Trap — Negative Base Verb Rule

After doesn't, always use the base form have, never has.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
She doesn't has a car.
She doesn't have a car.
4. Yes/No Questions (?) & Short Answers

Yes and No questions and short answers table for verb HAVE
Question (?)Positive Short AnswerNegative Short Answer
Do you have a car?Yes, I do.No, I don't.
Does he have a brother?Yes, he does.No, he doesn't.
Does she have a job?Yes, she does.No, she doesn't.
Do they have pets?Yes, they do.No, they don't.

⚠️ Common Trap — Question Base Verb Rule

When you use does, the main verb returns to its basic infinitive form, have.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
Does she has a cat?
Does she have a cat?
5. Wh- Questions with "Have"

items: **What:** <mark class="example-chip">What do you have in your bag?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">What do you have for breakfast?</mark>
**Who:** <mark class="example-chip">Who do you have in your family?</mark>
**How many:** <mark class="example-chip">How many brothers do you have?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">How many bedrooms does the house have?</mark>
**How much:** <mark class="example-chip">How much money do you have?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">How much time do we have?</mark>
**What colour:** <mark class="example-chip">What colour eyes does she have?</mark>
**What kind:** <mark class="example-chip">What kind of phone does he have?</mark>

blocks.text: 6. "Have got" vs "Do/Does Have"
Have got is common in informal English (especially British English) for possession, family, and physical features.

Comparison table between Have Got and Do/Does Have systems
StructureDo/Does + Have SystemHave got System
Affirmative (+)I have a car. / She has a cat.I've got a car. / She's got a cat.
Negative (-)I don't have a dog. / She doesn't have a car.I haven't got a dog. / She hasn't got a car.
Question (?)Do you have a pet? / Does she have a car?Have you got a pet? / Has she got a car?
Short AnswerYes, I do. / No, she doesn't.Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

⚠️ Common Trap — System Mixing

NEVER MIX THE TWO SYSTEMS:

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
Does she have got a car?
Does she have a car? OR Has she got a car?
7. Everyday Expressions & Illnesses with "Have"

items: **Daily Activities & Routines:** <mark class="example-chip">have breakfast / lunch / dinner</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a coffee</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a shower / bath</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a break</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a rest</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a party</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a good time</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a look</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a chat</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a holiday</mark>.

**Illnesses & Physical Conditions:** <mark class="example-chip">have a headache</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a stomachache</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a cold</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a fever</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">have a toothache</mark>.

**Countable vs Uncountable (some / any):**
  • Affirmative (+): <mark class="example-chip">I have some apples.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I have some water.</mark>
  • Negative (-): <mark class="example-chip">I don't have any apples.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I don't have any money.</mark>
  • Question (?): <mark class="example-chip">Do you have any questions?</mark>

blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes & Side-by-Side Comparisons
Contrast these key structures with 'to be' and 'to have':

STRUCTURE Meaning Type
EXAMPLE SENTENCE ✅
State / Feeling: (be + adjective)
I am hungry.
Possession: (have + noun)
I have a sandwich.
Activity: (have + meal)
I have breakfast at 8 AM.
9. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct negative form: 'She ___ a brother.'
blocks.explanation: After 'doesn't', the main verb always returns to its base form 'have'. 'She doesn't have a brother' is correct.

blocks.question: Which sentence correctly mixes 'have got' and 'do'?
options: Does she have got a car?
blocks.explanation: Never mix 'do/does' with 'got'. Use 'Has she got a car?' or 'Does she have a car?'

COSYMAGAZINE • Vol. 2026.08 — Special Edition

Verb 3 — "To Think"
To Think allows you to express your opinion, share your thoughts, and ask others for their view.
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb THINK
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI think it is a good idea. / You think too much. / We think English is fun. / They think it is easy.I don't think it is expensive. / You don't think about me. / We don't think it is a problem. / They don't think it is easy.Do you think it is good? / Do we think the same? / Do they think it is far?
He / She / ItShe thinks it is great. / He thinks about his family. / My brother thinks too fast.She doesn't think it is true. / He doesn't think about work.Does she think it is good? / Does he think about it?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -s Rule

Add -s with he, she and it in positive sentences. After doesn't or does, the verb goes back to think:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She think it is good.
She thinks it is good.
She doesn't thinks so.
She doesn't think so.
Does he thinks about it?
Does he think about it?
2. Think about, think of, think that

items: **think about** = keep something in your mind: <mark class="example-chip">I'm thinking about my holiday.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Think about it!</mark>
**think of** = have an idea or opinion: <mark class="example-chip">What do you think of this film?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I can't think of his name.</mark>
**think that** = give an opinion (that is optional): I think that it is a good plan. / I think it is a good plan.
**think so / don't think so** = short answers: <mark class="example-chip">Is it open? — I think so.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Is it cheap? — I don't think so.</mark>
**Natural English moves the negative:** we say <mark class="example-chip">I don't think she likes it.</mark> rather than <mark class="example-chip">I think she doesn't like it.</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Prepositions and "that"
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I think to my family.
I think about my family.
I think about that she is nice.
I think that she is nice.

Think for an opinion is a stative verb: say I think it is great., not I'm thinking it is great. But the activity "thinking" is fine: I'm thinking about my holiday.
3. Sentence Frames & Everyday Phrases

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **think** | He/She/It **thinks**.

**Expressing Opinions (I think that...):** <mark class="example-chip">I think it is a good idea.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I think learning English is fun.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She thinks this movie is great.</mark>
**Short Responses:** <mark class="example-chip">I think so.</mark> (I agree / I believe so) | <mark class="example-chip">I don't think so.</mark> (I disagree).
**Asking Opinions:** <mark class="example-chip">What do you think about this idea?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">What do you think of this film?</mark>

**Key Collocations:** <mark class="example-chip">think twice before deciding</mark> (be careful), <mark class="example-chip">think about the problem</mark> (consider), <mark class="example-chip">think of a solution</mark> (have an opinion/idea).

blocks.text: 4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Which sentence is correct?
blocks.explanation: With 'she', add -s to the verb: 'She thinks so.'

blocks.question: What is the natural way to say you disagree?
blocks.explanation: To disagree politely, say 'I don't think so.'

blocks.text:
💌 Your COSY journey

You can say who you are, what you have, and what you think. Ready to talk about what you know?

COSYMAGAZINE • Vol. 2026.08 — Special Edition

Verb 4 — "To Know"
The verb to know is essential for talking about facts, information, people, places, skills, and things we understand. In our logical sequence: first we think, and then we know!
The primary present simple forms are: • know — I, you, we, they • knows — he, she, it
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb KNOW
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI know the answer. / You know my brother. / We know this city well. / They know the truth.I don't know his name. / You don't know this place. / We don't know what to do. / They don't know anyone here.Do I know you? / Do you know the way? / Do we know the rules? / Do they know the price?
He / She / ItHe knows the teacher. / She knows the answer. / It knows the route.He doesn't know my address. / She doesn't know the truth. / It doesn't know any tricks.Does he know the time? / Does she know Peter? / Does it know where to go?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third Person Rule

Add -s to know only with he, she, and it in affirmative sentences.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
She know the answer.
She knows the answer.
2. Facts, Information & Embedded Question Words

items:
**A. Facts & Direct Information (Subject + know/knows + noun):**
  • <mark class="example-chip">I know the correct answer to question 5.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">She knows his full name and phone number.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">He knows the truth about what happened.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">We know the safety rules at work.</mark>

**B. Information with Question Words:**
  • <mark class="example-chip">I know where he lives in London.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">She knows what you want for your birthday.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">We know when the English lesson starts.</mark>
  • <mark class="example-chip">They know why he is angry today.</mark>

blocks.text: 3. Familiarity with People & Places

items: **A. People:** <mark class="example-chip">I know Anna from university.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She knows my older brother.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Do you know this man?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We don't know those people over there.</mark>

**B. Places:** <mark class="example-chip">I know this city very well.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He knows London like the back of his hand.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Do you know this Italian restaurant?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They don't know the area.</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Distinction — Knowing Someone

In English, knowing someone means you are familiar with them.
• I know Peter. = I am familiar with him.
• I meet Peter every day. = I encounter/see him every day.
• I know Peter well. = I am very familiar with him.
4. Negative Sentences (-) & "I don't know"
Use don't know or doesn't know. After doesn't, always use the base verb know, never knows.

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Form
TRY THIS ✅ Correct Form
He doesn't knows.
He doesn't know.

The Essential Phrase — "I don't know":
• “What's his name?” — “I don't know.”
• “Where is my phone?” — “I don't know.”
• Useful Variations: I really don't know. / I don't know yet. / I don't know why. / I don't know anything about it.
5. Yes/No & Wh- Questions (Embedded Word Order)
In embedded questions with Do you know...?, use statement word order (Subject + Verb).

INSTEAD OF ❌ Incorrect Order
TRY THIS ✅ Statement Order
Do you know where is the station?
Do you know where the station is?
Do you know what time is it?
Do you know what time it is?
Do you know who is she?
Do you know who she is?
6. "Know that" & "Know how to" (Skills)

items:
**A. Know (that) + sentence:** <mark class="example-chip">I know that you are tired.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She knows that he is French.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We know English is important.</mark> ('that' is optional in spoken English).
  • Negative contrast: <mark class="example-chip">I don't know that he is here.</mark> (lack of awareness) vs <mark class="example-chip">I don't know if he is here.</mark> (uncertainty).

**B. Skills (know how to + base verb):**
  • <mark class="example-chip">I know how to swim.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She knows how to cook Italian food.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He knows how to drive a car.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They don't know how to play chess.</mark>

**C. Know vs Know about:**
  • <mark class="example-chip">I know Maria.</mark> = I am acquainted with Maria personally.
  • <mark class="example-chip">I know about computers.</mark> = I have knowledge on the topic of computers.

blocks.text: 7. Stative Verb Rule & Comparisons

⚠️ Stative Verb Warning

Know describes a mental state, so it is not used in continuous tenses (-ing).

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I am knowing the answer.
I know the answer.

To talk about gradual familiarity, say: I am getting to know him.

Comparison table for mental state verbs think, know, and understand
VerbMeaningExample Sentence
thinkHave an opinion / beliefI think he is right.
knowHave factual certainty or familiarityI know he is right.
understandGrasp the meaning of somethingI understand what he says.
8. Key Daily Expressions with "Know"

items: **let someone know** = inform me (<mark class="example-chip">Let me know when you arrive!</mark>)
**get to know someone** = gradually become familiar (<mark class="example-chip">I want to get to know you.</mark>)
**as far as I know** = to my knowledge (<mark class="example-chip">As far as I know, the café is open.</mark>)
**know by heart** = memorize completely (<mark class="example-chip">I know this poem by heart.</mark>)
**know for sure** = be 100% certain (<mark class="example-chip">I don't know for sure.</mark>)

blocks.text: 9. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Which sentence has correct word order after 'Do you know...?'
options: Do you know where is the station?
Do you know where the station is?
Do you know where is station?
blocks.explanation: In embedded questions after 'Do you know...?', use normal statement word order: 'where the station is'.

blocks.question: Choose the correct skill structure: 'She knows ___ driving a car.'
blocks.explanation: For skills, use 'know how to + base verb': 'She knows how to drive a car.'

COSYMAGAZINE • Vol. 2026.08 — Special Edition

Verb 5 — "To Like" ❤️
After learning to be, to have, to think, and to know, let's master to like! This is a very useful verb for talking about things you enjoy, your hobbies, food, music, people, and preferences.
1. Preference Scale: Love, Like, Dislike & Hate

items: ❤️ **Love (❤️❤️❤️❤️❤️):** Enjoy very much ("I love chocolate!")
❤️ **Like (❤️❤️❤️):** Enjoy ("I like chocolate.")
👎 **Dislike (👎):** Not enjoy ("I dislike chocolate." — Note: *Dislike* sounds formal; in daily English, people usually say "I don't like chocolate.")
😠 **Hate (😠):** Dislike very strongly ("I hate cold weather." — Note: Be careful using *hate* with people, as it sounds harsh).

blocks.text: 2. Conjugation Table & The Third-Person Rule
To like is a regular verb. In the present simple, add -s for he, she, and it.

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb LIKE
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI like music. / You like pizza. / We like traveling. / They like concerts.I don't like coffee. / You don't like tea. / We don't like waiting. / They don't like noise.Do I like this? / Do you like tea? / Do we like this movie? / Do they like cooking?
He / She / ItHe likes sports. / She likes reading. / It likes milk.He doesn't like cold weather. / She doesn't like cats. / It doesn't like water.Does he like football? / Does she like dancing? / Does it like warmth?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -s Rule

Add -s with he, she, and it in positive sentences.

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She like pizza.
She likes pizza.

In negatives and questions, after doesn't or does, the main verb returns to base like:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She doesn't likes tea. / Does he likes football?
She doesn't like tea. / Does he like football?
3. What Can Come After "Like"?

items: **Pattern 1: Like + Noun:** <mark class="example-chip">I like Italian food.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She likes dogs.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They like classical music.</mark>

**Pattern 2: Like + Verb-ing:** <mark class="example-chip">I like swimming in the morning.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He likes cooking pasta.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We like watching films.</mark> (Emphasizes active enjoyment)

**Pattern 3: Like + to + Verb:** <mark class="example-chip">I like to read before bed.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She likes to dance.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They like to travel in summer.</mark> (Emphasizes habit or preference)

blocks.text:
⚠️ Distinction — Like vs Would Like

• I like coffee. = I enjoy coffee generally.
• I'd like a coffee. = I want a coffee now, politely. (Would like is covered on To Want!).
4. Related Verbs: Love, Dislike & Hate

The same grammar rules apply to love, dislike, and hate:
• I love my family. / She loves dancing.
• He dislikes waiting. (Or naturally: He doesn't like waiting.)
• My cat hates water. / They hate getting up early.
5. Everyday Expressions & Stative Verb Rule

items: **Intensity:** <mark class="example-chip">I really like it!</mark> (A lot) | <mark class="example-chip">I quite like it.</mark> (To some degree) | <mark class="example-chip">I don't like it very much.</mark>
**Polite Neutrality:** <mark class="example-chip">I don't mind.</mark> (It is okay / no objection) | <mark class="example-chip">It's not my cup of tea.</mark> (Idiom: Not something I enjoy)

blocks.text:
⚠️ Stative Verb Rule

Like describes a state or preference, so use present simple in standard English.

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I'm liking this song.
I like this song.
6. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence:
blocks.explanation: With 'she', use 'doesn't' followed by the base verb 'like' without an -s.

blocks.question: What does 'I'd like a glass of water' mean?
options: I want a glass of water, politely.
blocks.explanation: 'I'd like' means 'I would like', which expresses a polite desire right now, not a general hobby.

Verb 6 — "To Want / Would Like"
To Want and Would Like express desires, intentions, and polite requests.
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb WANT
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI want a coffee. / You want more time. / We want to travel. / They want a new car.I don't want any sugar. / You don't want to wait. / We don't want to be late. / They don't want help.Do you want some tea? / Do we want to leave now? / Do they want to come?
He / She / ItHe wants a new phone. / She wants to learn English. / My dog wants food.He doesn't want to go. / She doesn't want any coffee.Does he want some help? / Does she want to come?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -s Rule

Add -s with he, she and it. After doesn't or does, use want again:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She want a coffee.
She wants a coffee.
He doesn't wants to go.
He doesn't want to go.
Does she wants to come?
Does she want to come?
2. What can come after "want"?

items: **Pattern 1: want + noun:** <mark class="example-chip">I want a glass of water.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She wants a new bag.</mark>
**Pattern 2: want + to + verb:** <mark class="example-chip">I want to go home.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They want to learn English.</mark>
**Pattern 3: want + someone + to + verb:** <mark class="example-chip">I want you to come.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She wants him to help her.</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — "to" after want
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I want go home.
I want to go home.
I want that you come.
I want you to come.
3. Want vs Would Like

items: **Direct Desires (Want + Noun / Verb):** <mark class="example-chip">I want a glass of cold water.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I want to learn English fluently.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Where do you want to go tonight?</mark>
**Polite Standard (Would like + Noun / Verb):** <mark class="example-chip">I would like to order lunch now, please.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She would like a fresh salad.</mark>
**Negative Forms:** <mark class="example-chip">I don't want to be late for class.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He doesn't want to go home yet.</mark>

**Common Phrases:** <mark class="example-chip">if you want to come</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">I want to know the truth</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">we would like to see the museum</mark>.

blocks.text:
Want or would like by situation
SituationSayWhy
With friends and familyDo you want some tea? / I want a pizza.Direct and friendly.
In a café or restaurantI would like a coffee, please. / I'd like the soup.Polite and standard.
Offering somethingWould you like some water? / Would you like to sit down?Polite with guests and strangers.
Accepting or refusingYes, please. / No, thank you.Short and polite.

⚠️ Common Trap — Politeness

I want a coffee is correct, but with a waiter or a stranger it can sound blunt. Use I would like or I'd like. Notice the difference between Would you like a coffee? (an offer) and Do you like coffee? (a general question).
4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Which sentence is correct?
blocks.explanation: Add -s for 'he' and use 'to' before the next verb: 'He wants to go.'

blocks.question: Which is the most polite way to order a coffee?
blocks.explanation: 'I'd like ... please' is the standard polite form for ordering.

Verb 7 — "To Work / Study / Learn"
To Work, To Study, and To Learn are your core verbs for everyday occupations, education, and acquiring new skills.
Work, study and learn are regular verbs. With he, she and it: works, studies (study → studies), learns.
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verbs WORK, STUDY and LEARN
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI work in an office. / You study every evening. / We learn something new every day. / They work hard.I don't work on Sundays. / You don't study enough. / We don't learn fast. / They don't work here.Do you work here? / Do you study English? / Do they learn quickly?
He / She / ItShe works from home. / He studies medicine. / She learns quickly.She doesn't work on Fridays. / He doesn't study at night. / He doesn't learn from his mistakes.Does he work here? / Does she study law? / Does he learn fast?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -s Rule

Add -s (or -ies for study) with he, she and it. After doesn't or does, use the base verb:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She study English.
She studies English.
He doesn't works on Sunday.
He doesn't work on Sunday.
Does she learns fast?
Does she learn fast?
2. Prepositions & patterns

items: **work in / at / for / as:** <mark class="example-chip">I work in an office.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She works at a bank.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He works for a big company.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They work as nurses.</mark>

**study + subject** (no preposition): <mark class="example-chip">I study history.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He studies medicine.</mark> and **study for** an exam: <mark class="example-chip">We study for the test together.</mark>
**learn + noun or to + verb:** <mark class="example-chip">I learn English.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Children learn to swim quickly.</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Prepositions
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She works like a teacher.
She works as a teacher.
I study for be a doctor.
I study to be a doctor.
I work at the hospital as a nurse in.
I work at the hospital as a nurse.
3. Sentence Frames, Learn vs Teach and Everyday Phrases

items: **To Work (work / works):** <mark class="example-chip">I work in an office in London.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She works from home on Fridays.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They work hard every day.</mark> (Collocations: *work out*, *work full-time*, *work as a teacher*).

**To Study (study / studies):** <mark class="example-chip">I study English every evening.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He studies medicine at university.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We study for our exams together.</mark> (Note spelling: *study → studies*).

**To Learn (learn / learns):** <mark class="example-chip">I want to learn French fluently.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Children learn languages very quickly.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We learn something new every day.</mark> (Collocations: *learn by heart*, *learn from mistakes*).
**Key Nuance:** *Work* relates to employment and effort; *Study* relates to academic focus and coursework; *Learn* relates to acquiring new knowledge or competencies.

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Learn vs Teach
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She learns me English.
She teaches me English.

Learn is what the student does; teach is what the teacher does. Unlike like or know, these verbs are not stative: I'm studying for an exam this week. / I'm learning to cook. are natural.
4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence: "She ___ at a hospital."
blocks.explanation: With 'she', add -s: 'She works at a hospital.'

blocks.question: My teacher ___ us English.
blocks.explanation: The teacher teaches; the students learn.

Verb 8 — "To Go / Be Going To"
To Go expresses movement, travel, routines, and future intentions (be going to).
Go is irregular in the third person: goes (pronounced like goze).
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb GO
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI go to work by train. / You go to school early. / We go to the park on Sundays. / They go abroad every summer.I don't go to the gym. / You don't go out much. / We don't go by car. / They don't go home early.Do you go to school here? / Do we go this way? / Do they go to the market?
He / She / ItHe goes to the gym every day. / She goes to school by bus. / It goes very fast.He doesn't go to work on Sunday. / She doesn't go by car.Does he go to school? / Does she go to the park?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -es Rule

Use goes with he, she and it. After doesn't or does, go back to go:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She go to school.
She goes to school.
He doesn't goes to work.
He doesn't go to work.
Does she goes to the park?
Does she go to the park?
2. Go + place: "to" or no "to"?

items: **go to + place:** <mark class="example-chip">I go to school.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We go to the cinema.</mark>
**no "to"** with home, abroad, here, there, downtown, upstairs: I go home at six. / They go abroad every summer.

**go by + transport:** <mark class="example-chip">go by bus</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">go by train</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">go by car</mark> and <mark class="example-chip">go on foot</mark> (not "by foot").

**go + -ing** for activities: <mark class="example-chip">go swimming</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">go shopping</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">go running</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">go dancing</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Prepositions
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I go to home.
I go home.
I go by the bus.
I go by bus.
We go to shopping.
We go shopping.
3. Sentence Frames & Future Plans (be going to)

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **go** | He/She/It **goes**.

**Movement & Prepositions:** <mark class="example-chip">I go to work by train.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She goes to school every morning.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We go to the park on Sundays.</mark>

**Exceptions without 'to':** <mark class="example-chip">go home</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">go abroad on holiday</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">go downtown</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">go grocery shopping</mark>.
**Future Intentions (be going to + verb):** <mark class="example-chip">I am going to eat dinner with friends.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They are going to buy a new car next month.</mark>

**Transport Phrases:** <mark class="example-chip">go on foot</mark> (walk), <mark class="example-chip">go by bus</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">go by train</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">go by car</mark>.
**Affirmative:** <mark class="example-chip">I am going to call her.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She is going to travel next month.</mark>
**Negative:** <mark class="example-chip">I'm not going to be late.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They aren't going to come.</mark>
**Question:** <mark class="example-chip">Are you going to study tonight?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Is he going to cook?</mark>
**Short answers:** <mark class="example-chip">Yes, I am.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">No, I'm not.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Yes, he is.</mark>

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — be going to
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I going to eat dinner.
I am going to eat dinner.
She is going to eats.
She is going to eat.
4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence:
options: She go to school by bus.
She goes to school by bus.
She goes to school by the bus.
blocks.explanation: Use 'goes' with 'she' and 'by bus' without an article.

blocks.question: Tonight I ___ going to cook pasta.
blocks.explanation: 'I' goes with 'am': 'I am going to cook pasta.'

Verb 9 — "To Can" (Modal Verb)
Can is a modal verb expressing ability, permission, and polite requests.
Can has one form for every subject. No -s, no do/does, and no to before the next verb.
1. Forms & Conjugation Table

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verb CAN
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI can speak three languages. / You can sit here. / We can help you. / They can swim.I can't drive. / You can't park here. / We can't come tonight. / They can't hear you.Can I come in? / Can you help me? / Can we sit here? / Can they swim?
He / She / ItHe can play the guitar. / She can run fast. / It can fly.He can't swim. / She can't come today.Can he swim? / Can she help us?

⚠️ Common Trap — Can Never Changes

Can never takes -s, never takes to, and makes its own questions:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
She cans swim.
She can swim.
She can to swim.
She can swim.
Does she can swim?
Can she swim?
2. Three jobs for can

items: **Ability:** <mark class="example-chip">I can swim.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She can speak French.</mark>
**Permission, requests and offers:** <mark class="example-chip">Can I sit here?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Can you help me?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Can I help you?</mark>
**Possibility and senses:** <mark class="example-chip">I can see the sea.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">I can hear music.</mark>
**More polite:** Could you help me, please? / Could I have the bill? (could is softer than can).
**Short answers:** Yes, I can. / No, I can't. Cannot is written as one word and sounds formal.

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Short Answers and "to"
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
Yes, I can to.
Yes, I can.
I can't to come.
I can't come.
3. Sentence Frames & Useful Phrases

items: **Ability:** <mark class="example-chip">I can speak three languages.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She can swim very fast in the pool.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He can play the acoustic guitar.</mark>
**Negative Ability (cannot / can't):** <mark class="example-chip">I can't drive a manual car.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">She can't come to the party tonight.</mark>

**Requests & Permission:** <mark class="example-chip">Can you help me with this bag?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Can I have a glass of water?</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">You can sit here near the window.</mark>
**Useful Phrases:** <mark class="example-chip">as fast as I can</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">I can do it</mark>, <mark class="example-chip">Can I ask a quick question?</mark>

blocks.text: 4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: Choose the correct question:
blocks.explanation: 'Can' starts the question by itself: 'Can she swim?'

blocks.question: Which request is the most polite?
blocks.explanation: 'Could you ... please?' is the most polite.

COSYMAGAZINE • Vol. 2026.08 — Special Edition

Verb 10 — "To Eat / Drink"
To Eat and To Drink cover food, daily meals, dining habits, beverages, and hydration.
Eat and drink are regular verbs. With he, she and it: eats, drinks.
1. Forms & Conjugation Table (Present Simple)

Present simple conjugation and usage table for verbs EAT and DRINK
SubjectAffirmative (+)Negative (-)Question (?)
I / You / We / TheyI eat fruit every morning. / You drink a lot of water. / We eat dinner at eight. / They drink tea.I don't eat meat. / You don't drink coffee. / We don't eat late. / They don't drink milk.Do you eat breakfast? / Do you drink tea? / Do they eat fish?
He / She / ItHe eats lunch at one. / She drinks black coffee. / My cat eats fish.He doesn't eat sweets. / She doesn't drink juice.Does he eat meat? / Does she drink coffee?

⚠️ Common Trap — Third-Person -s Rule

Add -s with he, she and it. After doesn't or does, use the base verb:

INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
He eat fruit.
He eats fruit.
She doesn't drinks tea.
She doesn't drink tea.
Does she drinks tea?
Does she drink tea?
2. Some, any, a / an and a lot of

items: **Positive:** some or a lot of: I eat some fruit. / I drink a lot of water.
**Negative and questions:** any: I don't eat any meat. / Do you drink any coffee?
**Offers and requests:** some: Would you like some tea? / Can I have some water?
**Countable** (use a / an): an apple / a sandwich **Uncountable** (no article): water / rice / bread

blocks.text:
⚠️ Common Trap — Some, any and articles
INSTEAD OF ❌
TRY THIS ✅
I don't eat some meat.
I don't eat any meat.
I eat a rice.
I eat rice.
3. Sentence Frames, Meals and Invitations

items: **To Eat (eat / eats):** <mark class="example-chip">I eat fresh fruit every morning for breakfast.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He eats lunch at 1 o'clock at work.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Let's eat out tonight.</mark> (Phrases: *eat healthy*, *something to eat*).

**To Drink (drink / drinks):** <mark class="example-chip">I drink two litres of water every day.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">He drinks black coffee in the morning.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Would you like something to drink?</mark> (Phrases: *a hot drink*, *have a drink*).
**Social dining:** In English, we often say <mark class="example-chip">have breakfast / lunch / dinner</mark> or <mark class="example-chip">have a drink</mark> when socialising.
**Daily meals:** <mark class="example-chip">I have breakfast at seven.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">We have lunch at one.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">They have dinner late.</mark>
**Inviting:** <mark class="example-chip">Let's have a drink.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Let's eat out tonight.</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Would you like something to eat?</mark>
**At the table:** <mark class="example-chip">Help yourself!</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Enjoy your meal!</mark> / <mark class="example-chip">Cheers!</mark>

blocks.text: 4. Check Your Understanding

blocks.question: I don't eat ___ meat.
blocks.explanation: In negative sentences use 'any': 'I don't eat any meat.'

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence:
blocks.explanation: With 'she', add -s: 'She drinks water every day.'

⚠️ Be careful: one English verb, several words

English uses one verb where other languages need two or three. Be becomes ser or estar; know becomes savoir or connaître; like can be turned around (mi piace, gefällt mir, μου αρέσει). Learn each verb with its example sentence from your own language guide, not as a word-for-word swap. Forms for Breton, Armenian, Georgian, Bashkir, Chuvash and Tatar follow the guides of those languages.
Grammar & Structure Summary for A0–A1 / A2 Learners

• Simple Sentence Structures: Always maintain clear Subject + Verb + Object order. • Auxiliaries & Modals: Use 'can' for ability and 'would like' for polite requests. • Full Conjugations: Explore full present, past, and future conjugation tables across all 14 languages on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).
